98672.q: According to the sixth IPCC report, how much CO2 could still be emitted from the beginning of 2020 to keep to 1.5 °C with a 50 per cent probability?
98672.e: This remaining carbon budget corresponds to only just over a decade of today's emissions. It shrinks further every year.
98672.m: The remaining budget for 1.5 °C is very tight.

98673.q: Which special report did the IPCC publish in 2018 at the invitation of the 2015 Paris UN climate conference?
a: On the impacts of global warming of 1.5 °C
On the ice ages of the Alps
98673.e: The report compared the impacts of 1.5 °C and 2 °C of warming. It showed that even half a degree of difference has major effects.
98673.m: Every tenth of a degree of warming counts.

98674.q: What does a climate scenario such as RCP8.5 or RCP2.6 describe?
a: A possible course of greenhouse gases up to 2100
The weather forecast for next week
The number of weather stations worldwide
98674.e: RCP stands for Representative Concentration Pathway. The higher the number, the more greenhouse gases and the stronger the warming by 2100.
98674.m: The higher the number in the scenario, the stronger the warming.

98675.q: Apart from greenhouse gases, what else do the IPCC's SSP scenarios describe?
a: Possible developments in population, economy and technology
The Earth's orbit around the Sun
The height of the Alpine peaks
The position of the continents in millions of years
98675.e: SSP stands for Shared Socioeconomic Pathways. These social pathways are combined with climate forcings such as 2.6 or 8.5.
98675.m: SSP scenarios combine social development with climate forcing.

98676.q: Why is climate protection easier in a world with a lot of cooperation, education and careful use of resources?
a: Because emissions can be reduced more easily there
Because there is less sunshine there
Because greenhouse gases have no effect there
Because no energy is needed there
98676.e: In the SSP1 scenario the world focuses on sustainability. Climate protection and adaptation are then comparatively easy because countries work together and save resources.
98676.m: SSP1 is the pathway of sustainable development.

98677.q: What development is the SSP5-8.5 scenario based on?
a: Strong growth with high use of fossil energy
A rapid move away from coal, oil and gas
A sharp fall in the world's population
98677.e: SSP5 relies on technical progress and growth, driven mainly by fossil fuels. It leads to very high emissions.
98677.m: SSP5-8.5 is a scenario of very high emissions.

98678.q: According to the IPCC, roughly how much will the Earth warm by the end of the century if current trends continue?
98678.e: In the middle scenario SSP2-4.5 the best estimate is about 2.7 °C compared with 1850 to 1900. The Paris goal would clearly be missed.
98678.m: Carrying on as before leads to considerably more than 2 °C of warming.

98679.q: Which scenario of the sixth IPCC report is most likely to keep warming at around 1.5 °C by the end of the century?
98679.e: SSP1-1.9 assumes very rapid emission cuts and net zero CO2 around the middle of the century. The best estimate is 1.4 °C by the end of the century.
98679.m: Only very rapid emission cuts keep warming close to 1.5 °C.

98680.q: Why does the IPCC work with several emission scenarios instead of a single future?
a: Because future emissions depend on human decisions
Because the computers are too slow
Because every country has its own climate
98680.e: How much CO2 is emitted in future depends on politics, the economy and technology. Scenarios therefore show different possible paths.
98680.m: Scenarios show different possible climate futures.

98681.q: What are the climate scenarios for Switzerland that MeteoSwiss and ETH Zurich published in 2018 called?
98681.e: The scenarios show how temperature, rainfall and extremes in Switzerland could develop depending on the emissions pathway. Above all, they compare a future with consistent climate protection with a future without climate protection.
98681.m: Switzerland has its own regionally precise climate scenarios.

98682.q: What is the difference between an emissions scenario and a forecast?
a: It describes a possible future under certain assumptions
It predicts the future with certainty
It only relates to the past
It is based only on opinion polls
98682.e: Scenarios answer “what if” and do not give a probability of happening. Which path comes true depends on society's decisions.
98682.m: A scenario is an if-then statement about the future.

98683.q: At which university did the climate scientist Thomas Stocker head the Division of Climate and Environmental Physics from 1993?
98683.e: Stocker became a professor at the Physics Institute in Bern in 1993. The division is known for its work on ice cores.
98683.m: Thomas Stocker shaped climate physics in Bern.

98684.q: What role did Thomas Stocker have in the IPCC's fifth assessment report?
a: President of the World Meteorological Organization
98684.e: From 2008 to 2015 Stocker led the working group on the physical science basis together with a Chinese colleague. Its report appeared in 2013.
98684.m: A Swiss scientist co-led the science part of an IPCC report.

98685.q: What is the Bern climate scientist Thomas Stocker particularly known for?
a: For climate research with ice cores and his work in the IPCC
For the first ascent of Mount Everest
98685.e: Climate physics in Bern studies air bubbles in ice cores to reconstruct past climate. Stocker also led part of the fifth IPCC report.
98685.m: Thomas Stocker studies the climate using ice cores and worked in the IPCC.

98686.q: Which subject did Thomas Stocker study at ETH Zurich?
98686.e: Stocker completed his doctorate at ETH Zurich in 1987. After that he did research in London, Montreal and New York, among other places.
98686.m: Thomas Stocker is a physicist by training.

98687.q: In 2015 the Federal Council nominated Thomas Stocker to chair which international body?
98687.e: The Federal Council nominated Stocker as a candidate to chair the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. In the end, Hoesung Lee from South Korea was elected.
98687.m: In 2015 Switzerland put forward a candidate to chair the IPCC.

98688.q: Which important Swiss science prize did Thomas Stocker receive in 2017?
98688.e: The Marcel Benoist Prize is regarded as the most important science prize in Switzerland. It honoured Stocker's contributions to understanding the climate system.
98688.m: The Marcel Benoist Prize is Switzerland's highest science award.

98689.q: Which German polar explorer is the European Geosciences Union medal that Stocker received in 2026 named after?
98689.e: The Alfred Wegener Medal is one of the highest awards of the European Geosciences Union. Wegener explored Greenland and founded the theory of continental drift.
98689.m: In 2026 Stocker received the Alfred Wegener Medal.

98690.q: Which concept describes the opposite temperature trends in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres when the Atlantic circulation changes, as studied by Stocker?
98690.e: If the supply of heat to the North Atlantic weakens, the north cools while the south slowly warms. Ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica show this pattern.
98690.m: In the bipolar seesaw, north and south behave in opposite ways.

98691.q: Roughly what share of human CO2 emissions is taken up by the oceans and land ecosystems together?
98691.e: The other half builds up in the atmosphere. Without these natural sinks, the CO2 content would rise twice as fast.
98691.m: Natural sinks absorb about half of our CO2 emissions.

98692.q: What is the process called in which cold, CO2-rich surface water sinks and carries carbon into the depths?
98692.e: Cold water dissolves more CO2 and sinks at high latitudes. This brings dissolved carbon into the deep sea for a long time.
98692.m: The solubility pump carries CO2 into the depths with cold water.

98693.q: What is the transport of carbon into the deep sea by sinking remains of plankton called?
98693.e: Plankton binds CO2 through photosynthesis. Dead parts sink and hold carbon in the depths or in the sediment.
98693.m: Plankton pumps carbon into the depths of the sea.

98694.q: Which land habitat stores a particularly large amount of carbon worldwide on only about 3 per cent of the land area?
98694.e: In wet peatlands, plant remains hardly break down and build up as peat. Peatlands therefore store more carbon than all the forests on Earth put together.
98694.m: Intact peatlands are important carbon stores.

98695.q: When does a forest turn from a carbon sink into a carbon source?
a: When it gives off more CO2 than it takes up
When it is more than a hundred years old
When it has no leaves in winter
When it grows in the mountains
98695.e: Drought, fires or pests can make trees die. As the wood breaks down, more CO2 is released than the forest is still binding.
98695.m: A forest is only a sink as long as it binds more than it releases.

98696.q: What is the increased plant growth caused by a higher CO2 content in the air called?
98696.e: More CO2 makes photosynthesis easier for many plants. This explains part of the uptake by land ecosystems, but it is limited by water and nutrients.
98696.m: More CO2 makes plants grow more strongly in some cases.

98697.q: What is the technical process of filtering CO2 directly out of the surrounding air called?
98697.e: Fans suck air through filters on which CO2 is bound and later released in concentrated form. It can then be stored permanently, but the process uses a great deal of energy.
98697.m: Direct Air Capture removes CO2 from the air by technical means.

98698.q: 40 Gt of CO2 are emitted, half stays in the air, and 1 ppm corresponds to 7.8 Gt of CO2. By how much does the CO2 content rise?
98698.e: 40 : 2 = 20 Gt of CO2 stay in the air. 20 : 7.8 gives about 2.6 ppm.
98698.m: Without natural sinks the CO2 content would rise twice as fast.

98699.q: In climate policy, what is a process called that removes more greenhouse gas from the atmosphere than it releases?
98699.e: Sinks take up greenhouse gases and store them, for example in soils, biomass or seawater. Sources, on the other hand, give off greenhouse gases.
98699.m: A sink removes greenhouse gases from the atmosphere.

98700.q: Where does the water of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation mainly sink into the depths?
a: In the far North Atlantic, for example in the Labrador Sea
98700.e: There, salty surface water cools strongly and becomes heavy. It forms North Atlantic Deep Water, which flows south.
98700.m: In the far north of the Atlantic, heavy water sinks into the depths.

98701.q: Which unit measures volume flows in the ocean and equals one million cubic metres per second?
98701.e: The unit is named after the Norwegian oceanographer Harald Sverdrup. All the rivers in the world together carry only about one sverdrup of water.
98701.m: Ocean currents are measured in sverdrups.

98702.q: How much water does the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation move compared with all the rivers in the world together?
98702.e: At 26.5° north, the overturning circulation carries on average about 17 million cubic metres of water per second. All the rivers on Earth together carry only about 1 million cubic metres per second.
98702.m: The Atlantic current moves much more water than all rivers together.

98703.q: What does the sixth IPCC report expect for the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation in the 21st century?
a: A reversal of its direction of flow by 2030
98703.e: With medium confidence, the IPCC does not expect an abrupt collapse before 2100. But it does not completely rule one out.
98703.m: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation will probably weaken.

98704.q: Why does extra fresh water from Greenland weaken the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation?
a: It lowers the salt content and therefore the density of the surface water
It raises the temperature of the deep water
It slows down the Earth's rotation
98704.e: Less salty water is lighter and does not sink as easily. As a result, the driving force of the overturning becomes weaker.
98704.m: Fresh water makes seawater lighter and slows the sinking.

98705.q: What is the sea region south of Greenland that has cooled against the global trend called?
98705.e: The cold blob in the North Atlantic is often explained by a weaker supply of heat from the overturning circulation. Other causes are also being discussed.
98705.m: The cold blob in the North Atlantic could be a sign of weaker overturning.

98706.q: Why do researchers warn that the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation could tip?
a: It can have a strong and a weak stable state
The Earth's axis will soon flip
The Atlantic is slowly drying up
The Moon is slowing the current more and more
98706.e: Even Henry Stommel's simple model from 1961 showed that temperature and salt content work against each other. If a threshold is crossed, the current can switch into a weak state and stay there.
98706.m: Ocean currents can tip between two states.

98707.q: Which image is used to describe the worldwide overturning of the oceans, which distributes heat and salt?
98707.e: In the 1980s the researcher Wallace Broecker made the image of the global conveyor belt famous. It shows how water, heat and salt circulate between the oceans.
98707.m: The image of the conveyor belt made ocean circulation easy to picture.

98708.q: What effect does the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation have on the climate of north-western Europe?
a: It brings warmth and makes the winters milder
It brings cold water and cools the summers
98708.e: The current carries warm surface water north and releases heat into the air there. Westerly winds carry this heat to Europe.
98708.m: The Atlantic current is a heat pipeline to Europe.

98709.q: What do isomers always have in common?
98709.e: Isomers are compounds with the same molecular formula but a different structure. That is why they usually differ in their properties too.
98709.m: Isomers have the same molecular formula but a different structure.

98710.q: How many structural isomers are there for the molecular formula C5H12?
98710.e: There are n-pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane. No further branching is possible with five C atoms.

98711.q: Besides n-butane, which compound is the second isomer with the molecular formula C4H10?
98711.e: Like n-butane, 2-methylpropane (isobutane) has four C atoms and ten H atoms, but it is branched. Cyclobutane has only eight H atoms.

98712.q: Which compound is an isomer of ethanol (C2H6O)?
98712.e: Dimethyl ether (CH3-O-CH3) also has the molecular formula C2H6O but belongs to a different class of compounds. This is called functional group isomerism.
98712.m: Ethanol and dimethyl ether have the same molecular formula.

98713.q: Why does but-2-ene have a cis and a trans isomer?
a: The C=C double bond cannot rotate freely.
98713.e: The parts of the molecule cannot rotate freely around a double bond. That is why two fixed arrangements of the methyl groups are possible.
98713.m: A double bond prevents free rotation.

98714.q: What characterises the cis isomer of an alkene?
a: Identical substituents are on the same side of the double bond.
Identical substituents are on opposite sides.
The molecule has a triple bond.
The molecule cannot be superimposed on its mirror image.
98714.e: “Cis” means on this side, “trans” means across. In the cis isomer, the identical groups are on the same side of the double bond.
98714.m: In the cis isomer, identical groups are on the same side.

98715.q: What does the letter “Z” stand for in E/Z nomenclature?
98715.e: Z comes from the German word “zusammen”, meaning together: the highest-priority substituents are on the same side of the double bond. E stands for “entgegen”, meaning opposite.
98715.m: Z means together and E means opposite.

98716.q: How many structural isomers are there for the molecular formula C6H14 (hexane)?
98716.e: They are n-hexane, 2-methylpentane, 3-methylpentane, 2,2-dimethylbutane and 2,3-dimethylbutane. With each extra C atom, the number of isomers rises sharply.

98717.q: What are isomers called that have the same connections between atoms and differ only in their spatial arrangement?
98717.e: In stereoisomers the atoms are connected in the same way but arranged differently in space. Constitutional isomers, on the other hand, differ in how the atoms are connected.
98717.m: Stereoisomers differ only in their spatial arrangement.

98718.q: When is a molecule described as chiral?
a: when it cannot be superimposed on its mirror image
when it has a double bond
when it has a plane of symmetry
98718.e: A chiral molecule cannot be made to match its mirror image by any rotation. Molecules with a plane of symmetry, on the other hand, are achiral.
98718.m: Chiral molecules cannot be superimposed on their mirror image.

98719.q: What is a typical stereocentre in organic molecules?
a: a C atom with four different substituents
a C atom with a double bond
a C atom with two identical substituents
a C atom in a benzene ring
98719.e: A carbon atom with four different bonding partners is an asymmetric C atom. It is the most common cause of chirality.
98719.m: A C atom with four different groups is a stereocentre.

98720.q: Which Greek word does the term “chirality” come from?
98720.e: The Greek word “cheir” means hand. Left and right hands are mirror images that cannot be superimposed.

98721.q: Which of these molecules is chiral?
98721.e: In butan-2-ol, the second C atom carries H, OH, CH3 and C2H5, so four different groups. In propan-2-ol two groups are the same (two CH3).

98722.q: What is a compound called that has stereocentres but is still achiral because of an internal plane of symmetry?
98722.e: One example is meso-tartaric acid. Its two stereocentres cancel each other out because of the internal symmetry.
98722.m: A meso compound is achiral despite having stereocentres.

98723.q: Which proteinogenic amino acid is not chiral?
98723.e: In glycine, the side group is just a hydrogen atom. So the central C atom carries two H atoms and is not a stereocentre.
98723.m: Glycine is the only achiral proteinogenic amino acid.

98724.q: Which letters are used under the CIP rules to give the configuration of a stereocentre?
98724.e: Under the Cahn-Ingold-Prelog rules, the substituents are ranked by priority. Depending on the direction of rotation, the centre is labelled R (rectus) or S (sinister).
98724.m: The CIP rules distinguish R and S configurations.

98725.q: What is the maximum number of stereoisomers a molecule with 3 stereocentres can have?
98725.e: The maximum is 2 to the power of n. With three stereocentres that is 2 · 2 · 2 = 8.
98725.m: With n stereocentres there are at most 2 to the power of n stereoisomers.

a: Stereoisomers that relate to each other like an object and its mirror image
Molecules that differ only by rotation
98726.e: Enantiomers are mirror images that cannot be superimposed. They only occur in chiral molecules.
98726.m: Enantiomers relate to each other like an object and its mirror image.

98727.q: In which physical property do two enantiomers differ?
a: Direction in which they rotate plane-polarised light
98727.e: Enantiomers share almost all their physical properties. However, they rotate the plane of polarised light by the same amount in opposite directions.
98727.m: Enantiomers rotate polarised light in opposite directions.

98728.q: What is a mixture of equal parts of both enantiomers called?
98728.e: A racemate contains both enantiomers in a 1 to 1 ratio. Its optical activity is zero because the rotations cancel out.
98728.m: A racemate is a 1 to 1 mixture of both enantiomers.

98729.q: Who was the first to separate enantiomers in 1848 by sorting crystals of a tartaric acid salt by hand?
98729.e: Louis Pasteur noticed that the crystals had mirror-image shapes. The separated solutions rotated polarised light in opposite directions.
98729.m: Louis Pasteur discovered the handedness of molecules.

98730.q: For which substance does one enantiomer smell of caraway and the other of mint?
98730.e: (S)-carvone smells of caraway, (R)-carvone of spearmint. The smell receptors in the nose are chiral themselves and can tell the two forms apart.

98731.q: Which instrument is used to measure how much a solution rotates polarised light?
98731.e: In a polarimeter, polarised light passes through the sample and the angle of rotation is measured. This lets you identify enantiomers and their concentration.

98732.q: Which configuration do the amino acids in the proteins of living things almost always have?
98732.e: Living things build their proteins almost entirely from L-amino acids. D-amino acids only occur in exceptional cases, for example in bacterial cell walls.
98732.m: Proteins are made of L-amino acids.

98733.q: What are stereoisomers called that are not related as object and mirror image?
98733.e: Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images, for example cis and trans isomers. Unlike enantiomers, they have different physical properties.
98733.m: Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images.

98734.q: What happens in a substitution reaction?
a: An atom or group of atoms is replaced by another.
Atoms are added to a double bond.
A small molecule is split off from a molecule.
Two molecules combine without a by-product.
98734.e: “Substituere” means to replace. So in the molecule, one atom or group is swapped for another.
98734.m: In a substitution, part of the molecule is replaced.

98735.q: Which type of reaction takes place when methane reacts with chlorine in UV light?
98735.e: The light splits chlorine molecules into radicals. In a chain reaction, an H atom of methane is then replaced by a Cl atom.
98735.m: Alkanes react with halogens by radical substitution.

98736.q: What happens in the initiation step of the radical chlorination of alkanes?
a: Light splits chlorine molecules into chlorine atoms.
Two radicals combine to form a molecule.
Hydrogen chloride breaks down into ions.
98736.e: The energy of the light splits the Cl-Cl bond homolytically. This produces two chlorine radicals, each with one unpaired electron.
98736.m: Light starts the chain reaction by splitting chlorine molecules.

98737.q: Which inorganic by-product forms when chloromethane is made from methane and chlorine?
98737.e: The equation is CH4 + Cl2 gives CH3Cl + HCl. The replaced hydrogen atom combines with the second chlorine atom.

98738.q: What happens at the attacked stereocentre in an SN2 reaction?
98738.e: The nucleophile attacks from the back while the leaving group departs. The molecule flips over like an umbrella in the wind (Walden inversion).
98738.m: In an SN2 reaction, the configuration is inverted.

98739.q: Which intermediate occurs in an SN1 reaction?
98739.e: In SN1, the leaving group departs first, forming a positively charged carbocation. Only then does the nucleophile attack.
98739.m: The SN1 reaction goes via a carbocation.

98740.q: Which haloalkane is most likely to react by the SN1 mechanism?
98740.e: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is a tertiary haloalkane. It forms a particularly stable tertiary carbocation.
98740.m: Tertiary haloalkanes prefer to react by SN1.

98741.q: Why does benzene react with bromine by substitution rather than addition?
a: The aromatic electron system is kept.
Benzene has no electrons in double bonds.
98741.e: The aromatic system is particularly low in energy and stable. It is kept in a substitution but would be lost in an addition.
98741.m: Aromatic compounds prefer substitution because the aromatic system is kept.

98742.q: Which organic product forms when bromomethane reacts with sodium hydroxide solution?
98742.e: The hydroxide ion replaces the bromine atom: CH3Br + OH- gives CH3OH + Br-. This is a nucleophilic substitution.
98742.m: Haloalkanes react with alkali to form alcohols.

a: Atoms add to a multiple bond without forming a by-product.
One atom is replaced by another.
A small molecule is split off.
An ester is split with alkali.
98743.e: In an addition, a double or triple bond is broken. All the atoms of the reactants end up in the single product.
98743.m: In an addition, two molecules form a single product.

98744.q: How does the bromine water test show a C=C double bond?
a: The bromine water loses its colour.
98744.e: The brown bromine adds to the double bond. This forms a colourless dibromoalkane.

98745.q: Which product forms when bromine adds to ethene?
98745.e: One bromine atom bonds to each of the two C atoms of the former double bond. This forms 1,2-dibromoethane.

98746.q: Which product forms when hydrogen chloride adds to ethene?
98746.e: The H atom bonds to one C atom of the double bond and the Cl atom to the other. Ethene and HCl therefore give chloroethane.
98746.m: Ethene and hydrogen chloride give chloroethane.

98747.q: According to Markovnikov's rule, which main product forms from propene and hydrogen bromide?
98747.e: The H atom goes to the C atom that already carries more H atoms. The bromine atom therefore ends up on the middle C atom.
98747.m: According to Markovnikov, the C atom with more hydrogen gets the hydrogen.

98748.q: What is the addition of hydrogen to double bonds called, which is used to harden fats?
98748.e: In hydrogenation, hydrogen is added to C=C double bonds with a catalyst such as nickel. This turns liquid oils into firmer fats.
98748.m: Hydrogenation turns unsaturated fats into saturated ones.

98749.q: Which ring-shaped intermediate occurs when bromine adds to an alkene?
98749.e: The bromine molecule is polarised by the double bond. A three-membered ring with a positively charged bromine atom forms, which is then opened by a bromide ion.
98749.m: Bromine addition goes via a bromonium ion.

98750.q: Which plastic forms when a great many ethene molecules join through their double bonds?
98750.e: In polymerisation, the double bonds open and the ethene units link up to form long chains. Polyethylene is the most widely produced plastic.
98750.m: Ethene is polymerised to make polyethylene.

98751.q: How many moles of hydrogen are needed to fully hydrogenate 1 mol of ethyne to ethane?
98751.e: Ethyne has a triple bond. Going via ethene to ethane needs two addition steps, each with 1 mol of H2.
98751.m: A triple bond can take up two molecules of hydrogen.

98752.q: What happens in an elimination reaction?
a: A small molecule is split off from a molecule and a multiple bond forms.
Two molecules join and water is split off.
One atom is replaced by another.
A molecule is added to a double bond.
98752.e: Elimination means removal. Two neighbouring atoms or groups are split off and a double bond forms between them.
98752.m: Elimination is the reverse of addition.

98753.q: Which main product forms when ethanol is heated to about 170 °C with concentrated sulphuric acid?
98753.e: The sulphuric acid removes water from the ethanol. At high temperature, elimination produces the alkene ethene.
98753.m: Removing water turns ethanol into ethene.

98754.q: According to Zaitsev's rule, which alkene is mainly formed when HBr is eliminated from 2-bromobutane?
98754.e: According to Zaitsev, the more highly substituted, more stable alkene is preferred. In but-2-ene the double bond is in the middle of the chain.
98754.m: According to Zaitsev, the more stable, more highly substituted alkene is preferred.

98755.q: What is typical of an E2 elimination?
a: The elimination happens in a single step.
98755.e: In E2, the base removes a proton while the leaving group departs at the same time. There is no intermediate.
98755.m: The E2 reaction takes place in one step without an intermediate.

98756.q: With haloalkanes and bases, which type of reaction often competes with elimination?
98756.e: A base can also act as a nucleophile. Depending on the conditions, it replaces the halogen or splits off HX.
98756.m: Substitution and elimination often compete with each other.

98757.q: Which reagent is typically used to eliminate HBr from a bromoalkane?
98757.e: A strong base in alcoholic solution removes a proton and the bromide. This reaction is called dehydrohalogenation.
98757.m: Strong bases split hydrogen halides off haloalkanes.

98758.q: Which condition favours elimination over substitution?
98758.e: Elimination turns one particle into several, so entropy increases. High temperatures make this contribution more important.

98759.q: Which product forms when hydrogen bromide (HBr) is split off from bromoethane using a strong base?
98759.e: In the elimination, an H atom and the Br atom are removed from neighbouring C atoms. A double bond forms between the two C atoms, producing ethene.
98759.m: Splitting HBr off bromoethane gives ethene.

a: a particle with a lone pair of electrons that attacks positively polarised centres
a particle that is short of electrons
a particle with no charge and no electron pair
98760.e: A nucleophile provides an electron pair for a new bond. It therefore prefers to attack atoms with a partial positive charge.
98760.m: A nucleophile donates an electron pair.

98761.q: What does the word “nucleophile” literally mean?
98761.e: “Nucleus” is Latin for kernel or core, “philos” is Greek for loving. So a nucleophile seeks positive charge like that of an atomic nucleus.

98762.e: The hydroxide ion OH- is negatively charged and has lone pairs of electrons. The other three particles are electron-poor.
98762.m: The hydroxide ion is a typical nucleophile.

98763.q: In the Lewis acid-base concept, how can a nucleophile be described?
98763.e: A Lewis base is an electron pair donor. That is exactly what a nucleophile does when it forms a bond with a carbon atom.

98764.q: Which atom of a haloalkane is attacked by a nucleophile?
a: the C atom carrying the halogen
98764.e: The halogen is more electronegative than carbon. The bonded C atom is therefore positively polarised and attracts the nucleophile.
98764.m: Nucleophiles attack the positively polarised C atom.

98765.q: Which particle is an electrophile, the counterpart of a nucleophile?
98765.e: A carbocation has a positive charge on the carbon and is short of electrons. It is attacked by particles with a lone pair of electrons.
98765.m: Electrophiles are short of electrons, nucleophiles have a lone pair.

98766.q: Why is the hydroxide ion a stronger nucleophile than the water molecule?
a: because it carries a negative charge
because it has more hydrogen atoms
because it has no lone pair of electrons
98766.e: The negative charge makes the oxygen's electron pairs more readily available. Water is neutral and therefore a weaker nucleophile.

a: the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom
the positive charge on the nitrogen
the double bond in the molecule
the electron shortage on the hydrogen
98767.e: The nitrogen atom in ammonia has a non-bonding electron pair. This allows it to form amines with haloalkanes, for example.
98767.m: Ammonia attacks with its lone pair of electrons.

a: an electron-poor particle that attacks electron-rich sites
a particle that is always negatively charged
a particle that only reacts with metals
98768.e: “Electrophile” means electron-loving. Such particles accept an electron pair, for example from a double bond.

98769.e: The nitronium ion is positively charged and electron-poor. It attacks the electron system of benzene during nitration.
98769.m: Positively charged particles such as NO2+ are electrophiles.

98770.q: Which term from the Lewis acid-base concept fits an electrophile?
98770.e: A Lewis acid is an electron pair acceptor. An electrophile accepts an electron pair when it attacks.

98771.q: Which mixture is used to produce the nitronium ion for the nitration of benzene?
a: concentrated nitric acid and sulphuric acid
hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution
98771.e: The stronger sulphuric acid protonates the nitric acid. This then breaks down into water and the nitronium ion NO2+.
98771.m: Nitrating acid supplies the electrophile NO2+.

98772.q: What does an electrophile attack in an alkene?
a: the electrons of the C=C double bond
the neutrons in the carbon nucleus
a free bonding site on the hydrogen
98772.e: The double bond is a region of high electron density. That is where the electron-poor particle attacks.
98772.m: Electrophiles are attracted by double bonds.

98773.q: Why is a carbocation a strong electrophile?
a: Its positive C atom has only six valence electrons.
It has a lone pair of electrons.
98773.e: The positively charged carbon is one electron pair short of an octet. It therefore readily accepts an electron pair.
98773.m: A carbocation is two electrons short of an octet.

98774.q: Which reaction uses aluminium chloride to introduce an alkyl group into a benzene ring?
98774.e: Aluminium chloride turns a haloalkane into a strong electrophile. This replaces an H atom on the benzene ring.
98774.m: Friedel-Crafts alkylation attaches alkyl groups to aromatic compounds.

98775.q: What role does iron(III) bromide play in the bromination of benzene?
a: It polarises the bromine molecule and makes it a stronger electrophile.
It supplies the bromine atoms for the product.
It prevents hydrogen bromide from forming.
It breaks open the benzene ring.
98775.e: Benzene is too unreactive to react with pure bromine. The Lewis acid FeBr3 draws electrons away from the bromine and creates a strongly electrophilic bromine atom.
98775.m: A catalyst can strengthen a weak electrophile.

a: Two molecules join and a small molecule such as water is split off.
Water splits a molecule into two parts.
A double bond takes up hydrogen.
98776.e: In a condensation, a new bond forms between two molecules. At the same time, water is usually released.
98776.m: In a condensation, a small molecule is split off.

98777.q: Which bond forms when two amino acids undergo condensation?
98777.e: The carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amino group of the other, releasing water. This forms an amide bond, known as a peptide bond.
98777.m: Amino acids are linked by peptide bonds.

98778.q: Which plastic is made by polycondensation?
98778.e: Nylon is a polyamide made from a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid. A water molecule is released with each link.

98779.q: What is the reverse of a condensation called, in which a bond is split by water?
98779.e: In hydrolysis, water is taken up and a bond is split. This is how proteins are broken down during digestion, for example.
98779.m: Hydrolysis is the reverse of condensation.

98780.q: Which disaccharide forms when two glucose molecules condense via an α-1,4 bond?
98780.e: Maltose (malt sugar) consists of two glucose units. Sucrose, by contrast, contains glucose and fructose.
98780.m: Maltose consists of two glucose units.

98781.q: How many water molecules are split off when three amino acids form a tripeptide?
98781.e: Three building blocks need two peptide bonds. Each link releases one water molecule.
98781.m: With n building blocks there are n minus one peptide bonds.

98782.q: Which diol is condensed with terephthalic acid to make the plastic PET?
98782.e: PET stands for polyethylene terephthalate. It is made by polycondensation of terephthalic acid with ethanediol (ethylene glycol).
98782.m: PET is made from terephthalic acid and ethanediol.

98783.q: Which ether forms when two ethanol molecules condense with sulphuric acid at about 140 °C?
98783.e: Two ethanol molecules join through an oxygen atom and water is split off. The reaction temperature must be kept exactly.
98783.m: Two alcohol molecules can form an ether by splitting off water.

98784.q: Which substances react with each other in an esterification?
98784.e: A carboxylic acid and an alcohol form an ester. Water is the second product.
98784.m: Acid and alcohol give an ester and water.

98785.q: What is the ester made from acetic acid and ethanol called?
98785.e: The alcohol part (ethyl) comes first and the acid part (ethanoate) second. The substance is also called ethyl acetate and is a common solvent.
98785.m: Acetic acid and ethanol give ethyl ethanoate.

98786.q: Which substance is usually added as a catalyst in Fischer esterification?
98786.e: The acid protonates the carboxylic acid and makes it more reactive. Concentrated sulphuric acid also binds water.

98787.q: How can the yield of an esterification be increased?
a: by removing the water that forms
by adding the ester straight back
98787.e: Esterification is an equilibrium reaction. According to Le Chatelier's principle, removing a product shifts the equilibrium towards the ester side.
98787.m: Removing water shifts the equilibrium towards the ester.

98788.q: What are many short-chain esters used for in the food industry?
98788.e: Short-chain esters often smell fruity, for example of banana, apple or pineapple. That is why they are used as flavourings in sweets and drinks.

98789.q: Which alcohol is esterified with three fatty acids in fats?
98789.e: Glycerol (propane-1,2,3-triol) has three OH groups. Each one can form an ester with a fatty acid.
98789.m: Fats are esters of glycerol and fatty acids.

98790.q: Which functional group forms during esterification?
98790.e: The carboxyl group of the acid and the OH group of the alcohol combine and water is split off. This forms the ester group -COO-.

98791.q: Which painkiller is made by esterifying the OH group of salicylic acid?
98791.e: The phenol group of salicylic acid is converted into an acetyl ester using an acetic acid derivative. Acetylsalicylic acid is better tolerated than pure salicylic acid.
98791.m: Acetylsalicylic acid is an ester of salicylic acid.

98792.q: What is meant by saponification in chemistry?
a: splitting an ester with an alkali
forming an ester from an acid and an alcohol
98792.e: In saponification, an ester reacts with a base such as sodium hydroxide solution. This produces an alcohol and the salt of the carboxylic acid.
98792.m: Saponification is splitting an ester with alkali.

98793.q: Which products form when a fat is saponified with sodium hydroxide solution?
98793.e: The three ester bonds are split. Glycerol and the sodium salts of the fatty acids form, in other words soap.
98793.m: Fat and alkali give glycerol and soap.

98794.q: Unlike acidic ester hydrolysis, why is saponification practically irreversible?
a: The carboxylate ion that forms no longer reacts with the alcohol.
The alkali breaks down into hydrogen.
The ester is burnt to carbon dioxide.
98794.e: The carboxylic acid is immediately deprotonated by the alkali. The negatively charged carboxylate ion is too unreactive to form an ester again.
98794.m: Saponification goes to completion because the carboxylate does not react back.

98795.q: Which alkali is used to make soft soap?
98795.e: Potassium salts of fatty acids are soft and greasy. Sodium hydroxide solution, on the other hand, produces hard soap.
98795.m: Potassium hydroxide gives soft soap, sodium hydroxide gives hard soap.

98796.q: Why do you have to wear safety goggles and gloves when making soap with sodium hydroxide solution?
a: The alkali gives off poisonous chlorine gas
98796.e: Sodium hydroxide solution is a strong base and attacks skin and eyes. The soap only becomes mild once saponification is complete.
98796.m: Sodium hydroxide solution is corrosive, so you protect your eyes and skin.

98797.q: How many moles of sodium hydroxide are needed to fully saponify 1 mol of a fat (triglyceride)?
98797.e: A triglyceride contains three ester bonds. One hydroxide ion is used up for each.
98797.m: A fat molecule uses up three hydroxide ions during saponification.

98798.q: Which products form when ethyl ethanoate is saponified with sodium hydroxide solution?
98798.e: The hydroxide ion splits the ester bond. This produces the salt of acetic acid and the alcohol ethanol.
98798.m: Saponifying an ester gives a carboxylic acid salt and an alcohol.

98799.q: Which part of a soap anion is water-loving (hydrophilic)?
a: the methyl group at the end
98799.e: The negatively charged carboxylate group is surrounded by water molecules. The non-polar chain, by contrast, attaches itself to fat.
98799.m: Soaps have a water-loving head and a fat-loving tail.

98800.q: Under which brand name did thalidomide become known in Germany?
98800.e: Thalidomide was sold by the company Chemie Grünenthal as Contergan. The case is considered one of the biggest drug scandals.

98801.e: The company Chemie Grünenthal from Stolberg near Aachen introduced the drug on 1 October 1957. At the time it was thought to be especially well tolerated.

98802.q: What type of medicine was thalidomide originally sold as?
98802.e: Thalidomide was advertised as a harmless sleeping pill and sedative and was partly available without prescription. Severe side effects only came to light later.

98803.q: In which year was Contergan taken off the market?
98803.e: At the end of November 1961, Grünenthal withdrew the drug after it had been linked to severe harm in thousands of children.

98804.q: Why would giving only one pure enantiomer of thalidomide not have solved the problem?
a: The enantiomers convert into each other in the body.
A pure enantiomer cannot be made chemically.
Both enantiomers have no effect in the body.
Thalidomide has no stereocentre at all.
98804.e: Thalidomide has a stereocentre with an H atom that is easily removed. Under conditions in the body it racemises, so a pure enantiomer quickly turns back into both forms.

98805.q: Which disease is thalidomide used against today under strict conditions?
98805.e: Thalidomide inhibits the formation of new blood vessels and affects the immune system. That is why it is used against this bone marrow cancer and for certain complications of leprosy.
98805.m: Today thalidomide is used against bone marrow cancer.

98806.q: Is thalidomide still used as a medicine today?
a: Yes, under strict conditions against certain cancers
No, it is completely banned worldwide
Yes, as a sleeping pill without prescription
98806.e: Thalidomide inhibits the formation of new blood vessels and affects the immune system. That is why it is used under strict control against bone marrow cancer and for complications of leprosy.
98806.m: Today thalidomide is used under strict conditions against cancer.

98807.q: What consequence did the Contergan case have for the approval of medicines?
a: Medicines have had to be tested much more strictly ever since.
New medicines no longer need testing.
All sleeping pills were banned worldwide.
Chiral active ingredients may no longer be sold.
98807.e: Many countries then tightened their laws and required extensive tests before approval. The case is seen as a turning point in drug safety.
98807.m: The Contergan case led to stricter approval rules.

98808.q: What does it mean that thalidomide is a chiral molecule?
a: It exists in two mirror-image forms
It is completely insoluble in water
98808.e: Chiral molecules behave like left and right hands: they are mirror images but cannot be superimposed. The two forms are called enantiomers.
98808.m: Chiral molecules exist in two mirror-image forms.

98909.q: Which programming language is considered the first object-oriented language?
98909.e: Simula 67 was developed in the 1960s in Norway by Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard. It introduced classes and objects.
98909.m: Simula from Norway was the first object-oriented language.

98910.q: What is the OOP principle called in which an object's internal data is hidden from direct access from outside?
98910.e: With encapsulation, you only access an object's data through defined methods. This keeps the internal state protected.
98910.m: Encapsulation protects an object's data from direct access.

98911.q: What is the ability called whereby the same method call triggers different behaviour depending on the type of object?
98911.e: Polymorphism means “having many forms”. A call such as draw() can have a different effect for a circle than for a rectangle.
98911.m: Polymorphism lets the same call work differently depending on the object.

98912.q: Which computer scientist coined the term “object-oriented” and helped develop Smalltalk?
98912.e: Alan Kay helped develop Smalltalk at Xerox PARC in the 1970s. He is seen as the originator of the term object-oriented programming.
98912.m: Alan Kay coined the term object-oriented.

98913.q: In OOP, what do you call the functions that belong to an object?
98913.e: Methods describe an object's behaviour. Attributes, on the other hand, store its state.
98913.m: Methods determine what an object can do.

98914.q: In OOP, what do you call the data that stores an object's state?
98914.e: Attributes or fields record an object's properties, such as colour or size. Their values make up the object's state.

a: Same name, redefined in the subclass
The method is called too often
The method has no return value
98915.e: With overloading, there are several methods with the same name but different parameter lists. The compiler chooses the right one based on the arguments.
98915.m: Overloaded methods differ in their parameters.

98916.q: Which principle hides unimportant details and shows only what is essential about an object?
98916.e: Abstraction models only the properties that matter for the program. Complex details stay hidden.
98916.m: Abstraction shows only what is essential about an object.

98917.q: What do you call a concrete object created from the blueprint of a class?
98917.e: A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance of that class. You can create many instances from one class.
98917.m: An object is an instance of its class.

98918.q: Which special method is called automatically when an object is created?
98918.e: The constructor initialises the new object, for example by setting the starting values. In Java it has the name of the class.
98918.m: The constructor prepares a new object.

98919.q: In Python, which method is a class's initialiser?
98919.e: In Python, __init__ is called automatically after a new object has been created. That is typically where you set the starting values of the attributes.
98919.m: In Python, __init__ initialises a new object.

98920.q: What is true of an abstract class?
a: It must not be inherited from
98920.e: An abstract class serves as a template for subclasses. Only a concrete subclass that implements all the abstract methods can be instantiated.
98920.m: You cannot create an object directly from an abstract class.

98921.q: What is an attribute called that belongs to the class itself and is shared by all instances?
98921.e: A class variable, marked static in Java, exists only once per class. All objects see the same value.
98921.m: All objects of a class share a class variable.

98922.q: Which access modifier in Java allows access only within the class itself?
98922.e: With private, an attribute or method is only visible in its own class. This supports encapsulation.
98922.m: Private elements are only visible in their own class.

98923.q: Which design pattern ensures that there is exactly one instance of a class?
98923.e: The singleton pattern prevents further instances, often with a private constructor. It is one of the “Gang of Four” patterns.
98923.m: A singleton has exactly one instance.

98924.q: In Python, what is the usual name of the first parameter of an instance method?
98924.e: In Python, the current object is passed explicitly as the first parameter, called self by convention. In Java and C++, the corresponding reference is called this.
98924.m: In Python, self refers to the current object.

98925.q: With which keyword does a class inherit from another class in Java?
98925.e: In Java you write class Dog extends Animal. For interfaces, on the other hand, you use implements.
98925.m: In Java, you inherit with extends.

98926.q: In Java, which class does every class inherit from, directly or indirectly?
98926.e: java.lang.Object is at the top of the class hierarchy. That is why every object has methods such as toString().
98926.m: In Java, every class descends from Object.

98927.q: Which language allows multiple inheritance of classes?
98927.e: In C++, a class can inherit from several base classes. Java and C# only allow single inheritance for classes, but several interfaces.
98927.m: C++ has multiple inheritance of classes.

98928.q: What is the problem called when a class inherits from the same base class by two routes?
98928.e: If B and C inherit from A and D inherits from B and C, it is unclear which version of A's methods applies. The shape of the hierarchy looks like a diamond.
98928.m: The diamond problem arises with multiple inheritance by two routes.

98929.q: What do you call it when a subclass re-implements an inherited method with the same signature?
98929.e: With overriding, the subclass replaces the behaviour of the superclass. In Java you can mark this with @Override.
98929.m: With overriding, a subclass replaces an inherited method.

98930.q: Which relationship between subclass and superclass does inheritance express?
98930.e: A dog is an animal, so Dog can inherit from Animal. The has-a relationship, on the other hand, describes composition.

98931.q: After which computer scientist is the substitution principle for subclasses named?
98931.e: The Liskov substitution principle requires that objects of a subclass can be used anywhere in place of the superclass. It is the L in SOLID.
98931.m: The Liskov principle requires that subclasses can be substituted.

98932.q: Which Java keyword prevents a class from being inherited from?
98932.e: A class declared final cannot have subclasses. One example is the String class.
98932.m: A final class cannot be inherited from.

98933.q: With which keyword do you call the superclass constructor in Java?
98933.e: In Java, super(...) must be the first statement in the subclass constructor. In C#, the counterpart is called base.
98933.m: In Java, you reach the superclass with super.

98934.q: In version control, what do you call saving a set of changes with a description?
98934.e: A commit records a state of the files together with author, time and message. This makes the history traceable.
98934.m: A commit saves a set of changes permanently.

98935.q: Which of these systems is a centralised version control system?
98935.e: With Subversion (SVN), the history is on a central server. Git, Mercurial and Bazaar are distributed systems in which every copy contains the whole history.
98935.m: Subversion works with a central server.

98936.q: What do you call a parallel line of development in version control?
98936.e: In a branch, you can develop changes independently of the main branch. Later the branches are merged again.
98936.m: A branch is a separate line of development.

98937.q: What arises when two people have changed the same line of a file differently and the changes are merged?
98937.e: The system cannot decide automatically which change applies. A person has to resolve the conflict by hand.
98937.m: Contradictory changes lead to a merge conflict.

98938.q: What do you call a fixed marker for a particular state, for example for version 1.0?
98938.e: A tag points permanently to a particular commit. It is often used for release numbers.
98938.m: A tag marks a particular version.

98939.q: Who developed the version control system Git in 2005?
98939.e: Linus Torvalds, the creator of Linux, wrote Git for developing the Linux kernel. Today Git is the most widely used version control system.

98940.q: What do you call the storage location where a version control system keeps all files and their history?
98940.e: The repository contains all versions and metadata of a project. In distributed systems, every copy has a complete repository.
98940.m: The repository holds the whole history of a project.

98941.q: What is a big advantage of distributed version control over centralised version control?
98941.e: Because every local copy contains the whole history, you can also commit and look at histories offline. Syncing happens later.
98941.m: Distributed version control lets you work without a server.

98942.e: Linus Torvalds wrote Git for developing the Linux kernel. The reason was that BitKeeper, which had been used until then, was no longer available free of charge.

98943.q: What is a commit in Git?
a: A saved state of the project with a description
A new branch of the project
98943.e: With git commit, you save the staged changes as a new state in the repository. Every commit has a message and a unique ID.
98943.m: A commit records a state of the project.

98944.q: Which command adds changes to the staging area in Git?
98944.e: With git add, changes are staged for the next commit. Only git commit saves them in the repository.
98944.m: With git add, you stage changes for the commit.

98945.q: Which two steps does the command git pull combine?
98945.e: git pull first fetches changes from the remote repository (fetch) and then brings them into the current branch (merge). With an option, rebase can be used instead of merge.
98945.m: git pull fetches changes and merges them.

98946.q: With which hash function does Git identify its objects by default?
98946.e: Every commit has a 40-character hexadecimal SHA-1 checksum. Newer Git versions also support SHA-256.
98946.m: Git labels commits with SHA-1 hashes.

98947.q: In which file do you specify which files Git should not track?
98947.e: Patterns in .gitignore, such as *.log, exclude files from version control. Typical examples are build folders or password files.
98947.m: The .gitignore file excludes files from Git.

98948.q: Which Git command puts current changes aside temporarily without committing them?
98948.e: git stash stores the unfinished state on a stack and restores a clean working directory. With git stash pop you get it back.
98948.m: git stash puts changes aside temporarily.

98949.q: Which company bought the GitHub platform in 2018?
98949.e: Microsoft took over GitHub in 2018 for about 7.5 billion US dollars in shares. GitHub is one of the largest platforms for Git repositories.
98949.m: GitHub has belonged to Microsoft since 2018.

98950.q: In Git, what is the pointer to the currently checked-out commit or branch called?
98950.e: HEAD usually refers to the current branch and thus to its latest commit. With a “detached HEAD”, it points directly to a commit.
98950.m: HEAD points to the current state in Git.

98951.q: What do you call tests that check a program only through inputs and outputs, without knowing the code?
98951.e: In a black-box test, you test against the specification. The internal structure of the program is not considered.
98951.m: A black-box test only checks external behaviour.

98952.q: Which test checks whether parts that already worked still work correctly after a change?
98952.e: A regression test repeats existing tests after changes. This shows up unintended side effects.
98952.m: Regression tests find bugs newly caused by changes.

98953.q: Who said, in effect, that testing can show the presence of bugs but never their absence?
98953.e: With this, the Dutch computer scientist Edsger W. Dijkstra stressed the limits of testing. To be sure there are no bugs, you need formal proofs.
98953.m: Tests can show bugs but cannot prove there are none.

98954.q: What is the testing method called that specifically checks values at the edges of valid ranges?
98954.e: Mistakes often happen at range boundaries, for example using “less than” instead of “less than or equal to”. That is why you test values right at, below and above the boundary.
98954.m: Boundary value analysis tests the edges of value ranges.

98955.q: Which level of testing checks how several components work together?
98955.e: After the individual modules, you test whether their interfaces fit together. System and acceptance tests follow after that.
98955.m: The integration test checks how components work together.

98956.q: Which test is typically carried out by the customer to formally accept the software?
98956.e: In the acceptance test, the client checks whether the agreed requirements are met. After that, the software counts as accepted.
98956.m: With the acceptance test, the customer accepts the software.

98957.q: What do you call the measure of what share of the source code is executed by tests?
98957.e: Test coverage, also called code coverage, is often given as a percentage. But high coverage does not guarantee that there are no bugs.
98957.m: Test coverage shows how much code is tested.

98958.q: Which method divides inputs into groups that probably behave the same and tests one representative of each?
98958.e: You assume that all values in a class are treated the same. This greatly reduces the number of test cases needed.
98958.m: Equivalence classes save test cases by using typical representatives.

98959.q: What is the usual English name for a module test?
98959.e: A unit test checks the smallest testable unit, such as a single function or method. It usually runs automatically.
98959.m: A module test is usually called a unit test.

98960.q: Which Swiss computer scientist wrote the Java test framework JUnit together with Kent Beck?
98960.e: Erich Gamma and Kent Beck wrote JUnit in the 1990s. Gamma is also one of the four authors of the “Gang of Four” book on design patterns.
98960.m: The Swiss Erich Gamma helped develop JUnit.

98961.q: What do you call a stand-in object that simulates a real dependency in unit tests and checks calls?
98961.e: A mock replaces a database, for example, and checks whether it is called correctly. This keeps the test isolated and fast.
98961.m: A mock object replaces real dependencies in a test.

98962.q: What is the statement called with which a unit test checks an expected value?
98962.e: An assertion such as assertEquals compares the actual value with the expected one. If they do not match, the test fails.
98962.m: With an assertion, a test checks the expected result.

98963.q: What are the three phases of test-driven development?
98963.e: First you write a failing test (red), then the simplest code that makes it pass (green). After that you improve the code.
98963.m: Test-driven development follows the cycle red, green, refactor.

98964.q: What does test coverage (code coverage) indicate?
a: What share of the code is executed by the tests
How many bugs the code contains
How many people have checked the code
98964.e: Coverage of 80 per cent means that the tests run through 80 per cent of the lines of code. That does not make the code free of bugs.
98964.m: High test coverage does not automatically mean bug-free code.

98965.q: Which module of the Python standard library is used for writing unit tests?
98965.e: unittest has been in the standard library since Python 2.1 and is modelled on JUnit. pytest is popular but has to be installed separately.
98965.m: Python comes with the unittest module for unit tests.

98966.q: Which property should a good unit test have?
98966.e: Good unit tests are isolated, fast and repeatable. Their result must not depend on which tests ran before.
98966.m: Good unit tests run independently of each other.

98967.q: In which year was the Agile Manifesto published?
98967.e: In February 2001, 17 software developers met in Snowbird in the US state of Utah. There they drew up the Manifesto for Agile Software Development.
98967.m: The Agile Manifesto was written in 2001.

98968.q: Who wrote the Agile Manifesto in 2001?
98968.e: 17 experienced software developers, including Kent Beck and Martin Fowler, met at a ski resort in Utah in 2001. They were looking for shared values for lighter, more flexible methods of software development.
98968.m: The Agile Manifesto comes from developers working in practice.

98969.q: What does the Agile Manifesto value more highly than comprehensive documentation?
98969.e: One of the four values is: working software over comprehensive documentation. Documentation remains valuable but is less important.
98969.m: Agile teams put working software above documentation.

98970.q: How many principles go with the four values of the Agile Manifesto?
98970.e: The manifesto has twelve principles, such as early and continuous delivery of valuable software. They make the four values more concrete.
98970.m: The Agile Manifesto has four values and twelve principles.

98971.q: Which classic process model with strictly consecutive phases is seen as the counterpart to agile methods?
98971.e: In the waterfall model, analysis, design, implementation and testing follow one after another. Agile methods, by contrast, work in short cycles.
98971.m: The waterfall model works through its phases strictly one after another.

98972.q: Which agile method, shaped by Kent Beck, relies among other things on pair programming?
98972.e: Extreme Programming (XP) stresses practices such as pair programming, test-driven development and short releases. Kent Beck described them at the end of the 1990s.
98972.m: Extreme Programming relies on pair programming.

98973.q: What do you call a short requirement from the user's point of view, such as “As a customer, I want ...”?
98973.e: A user story briefly describes who wants what and why. It is a common format for requirements in agile teams.
98973.m: A user story describes a requirement from the user's point of view.

98974.q: Which agile method shows work on a board and limits the number of tasks in progress at the same time?
98974.e: Kanban originally comes from production at Toyota. In software, it limits the work in progress (WIP limit).
98974.m: Kanban limits the number of tasks at the same time.

98975.q: Which role in Scrum is responsible for the product backlog and for maximising the value of the product?
98975.e: The Product Owner orders and maintains the product backlog. They decide what is implemented next.
98975.m: The Product Owner is responsible for the product backlog.

98976.q: What is the maximum length of a sprint in Scrum?
98976.e: According to the Scrum Guide, a sprint has a fixed length of at most one month. Two weeks is common.
98976.m: A sprint lasts at most one month.

98977.q: According to the Scrum Guide, what is the maximum length of the Daily Scrum?
98977.e: The Daily Scrum is a short daily meeting of the developers with a timebox of 15 minutes. It is used to plan the next 24 hours.
98977.m: The Daily Scrum lasts at most 15 minutes.

98978.q: Which role in Scrum supports the team, removes obstacles and makes sure Scrum is understood?
98978.e: The Scrum Master is a servant leader. They help the team and the organisation to use Scrum effectively.
98978.m: The Scrum Master removes obstacles for the team.

98979.q: What kind of process model is Scrum?
98979.e: Scrum works in short sprints and keeps adapting the planning. It was presented in 1995 by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland.
98979.m: Scrum was presented by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland.

98980.q: Which sport does the term “scrum” come from?
98980.e: In rugby, a scrum is the tightly packed formation of players. In 1986, Takeuchi and Nonaka compared product development to a rugby team.
98980.m: The term scrum comes from rugby.

98981.q: Which event closes a sprint and is used to improve how the team works together?
98981.e: The retrospective follows the sprint review. The team thinks about what went well and what it wants to improve.
98981.m: In the retrospective, the team improves its way of working.

98982.q: What is the shared agreement called on when a piece of work counts as finished in Scrum?
98982.e: The Definition of Done sets quality criteria for the increment. Only when they are met does a piece of work count as done.
98982.m: The Definition of Done sets out when something is finished.

98983.q: What is the usable result of work created during a sprint in Scrum called?
98983.e: Along with the product backlog and the sprint backlog, the increment is one of the three Scrum artefacts. It must meet the Definition of Done.
98983.m: At the end of a sprint there is a usable increment.

98984.q: What is the Unified Modeling Language (UML) used for?
a: To describe software with standardised diagrams
98984.e: UML is a graphical language for classes, processes and use cases. It is maintained as a standard by the Object Management Group (OMG).
98984.m: UML is maintained by the Object Management Group.

98985.q: How are classes shown in a UML class diagram?
a: As a rectangle with name, attributes and methods
As an ellipse with a stick figure
As a circle with a number
98985.e: The rectangle has three sections: the class name at the top, the attributes in the middle and the methods at the bottom. UML grew out of the methods of Booch, Rumbaugh and Jacobson.
98985.m: In UML, a class is a rectangle divided into three.

98986.q: Which symbol stands for a private attribute in a UML class diagram?
98986.e: In UML, a plus sign (+) means public, a minus sign (-) private, a hash (#) protected and a tilde (~) package. The symbol comes before the attribute name.
98986.m: In UML, a minus sign marks private elements.

98987.q: How is inheritance shown in a UML class diagram?
a: Arrow with an empty triangular head
98987.e: Generalisation is shown by a solid arrow with a hollow triangle pointing from the subclass to the superclass. Diamonds stand for aggregation and composition.
98987.m: UML shows inheritance with a hollow triangle arrow.

98988.q: Which UML diagram shows the sequence of messages between objects over time?
98988.e: In a sequence diagram, lifelines run vertically and messages run horizontally as arrows. Time runs from top to bottom.
98988.m: A sequence diagram shows the flow of messages over time.

98989.q: What does a line with a filled diamond stand for in UML?
98989.e: In composition, the part cannot exist without the whole. The empty diamond stands for the weaker aggregation.
98989.m: A filled diamond shows composition in UML.

98990.q: Which UML diagram shows actors and the functions a system provides for them?
98990.e: The use case diagram shows actors as stick figures and use cases as ellipses. It describes the system from the user's point of view.
98990.m: A use case diagram shows actors and their use cases.

98991.q: Into which two main groups does UML divide its diagrams?
98991.e: Structure diagrams such as the class diagram show how something is built. Behaviour diagrams such as the sequence diagram show processes. UML 2.5 has seven of each.
98991.m: UML 2.5 defines fourteen types of diagram.

98992.q: What does the abbreviation API stand for?
98992.e: An API is a programming interface through which programs communicate with each other. It sets out which functions are called and how.

98993.q: What is typical of a REST API?
a: Every resource has its own address (URL)
All data is sent in XML envelopes
The server remembers every client permanently
There is only one single function
98993.e: In REST, resources such as /customers/42 can be reached at their own URLs and are handled with HTTP methods. Roy Fielding described the style in 2000.
98993.m: In REST, every resource has its own URL.

98994.q: Which HTTP method does a REST API usually use to read a resource?
98994.e: GET reads data without changing it. POST typically creates, PUT replaces and DELETE deletes resources.
98994.m: You read data from a REST API with GET.

98995.q: Which data format is most often used for exchanging data in modern web APIs?
98995.e: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is easy to read and can be processed by almost all languages. It consists of key-value pairs and lists.
98995.m: Modern web APIs mostly exchange data as JSON.

98996.q: Which older protocol for web APIs packs messages into XML envelopes?
98996.e: SOAP messages consist of an XML envelope with a header and a body. The interface is often described with WSDL.
98996.m: SOAP packs API messages into XML envelopes.

98997.q: What do you call limiting how many requests a client may make to an API in a period of time?
98997.e: Rate limiting protects a service against overload and misuse. When the limit is exceeded, many APIs reply with status code 429.
98997.m: Rate limiting limits the number of API requests.

98998.q: How did the US Supreme Court rule in 2021 in Google v. Oracle on the use of the Java API?
a: As a breach of competition law
98998.e: Google had recreated parts of the Java API for Android. The court ruled that this was permitted as fair use.
98998.m: The US court judged Google's use of the Java API to be fair use.

98999.q: What do you call an API function that still works but is to be removed in future?
98999.e: Functions marked as deprecated should no longer be used in new code. This gives developers time to switch.
98999.m: A deprecated function will be removed in future.

99000.q: Who wrote the GNU General Public License?
99000.e: Richard Stallman wrote the GPL for the GNU project. The first version came out in 1989.
99000.m: Richard Stallman is the author of the GPL.

99001.q: Are you allowed to sell software that is under the GPL?
a: Yes, if the source code is supplied under the GPL
No, it must always be free of charge
Only with permission from the Free Software Foundation
Only if you encrypt the code first
99001.e: With the GPL, free means freedom, not free of charge. You may charge money, but you must give buyers the source code and the same rights.
99001.m: You may sell GPL software, but the freedoms remain.

99002.q: What is the GPL principle called that derived works must be passed on under the same conditions?
99002.e: Copyleft uses copyright to secure freedom. Anyone who changes and distributes GPL software must also release the changes under the GPL.
99002.m: Copyleft requires the same freedoms for derived works.

99003.q: Under which licence is the Linux kernel?
99003.e: Linus Torvalds put Linux under the GPL in 1992. The kernel still uses version 2 of the GPL today.
99003.m: The Linux kernel is under GPL version 2.

99004.q: What does the recursive abbreviation GNU stand for?
99004.e: The GNU project wanted to create a free, Unix-like operating system. The name stresses that it is not Unix.

99005.e: The Free Software Foundation was founded by Richard Stallman in 1985. It is the publisher of the GPL.
99005.m: The Free Software Foundation publishes the GPL.

99006.q: According to the GPL, what must you do if you pass on a GPL program in compiled form?
99006.e: Anyone who distributes GPL software as a binary program must offer the recipients the source code. This keeps the software freely changeable.
99006.m: With GPL software, the source code must be available.

99007.q: Which licence, unlike the GPL, allows changed code to be passed on as closed software too?
99007.e: The MIT licence is permissive and has no copyleft. You only have to keep the licence notice, but you may build the code into your own closed programs.
99007.m: Permissive licences such as MIT do not require copyleft.

99008.q: How many basic freedoms does the Free Software Foundation define for free software?
99008.e: The four freedoms are numbered 0 to 3: to use, to study and change, to pass on, and to pass on improved versions. The GPL protects them.

99009.q: Which flower is often called the “queen of flowers”?
99009.e: The rose has been one of the most popular flowers for a very long time. That is why it is often called the queen of flowers.
99009.m: The rose is known as the queen of flowers.

99010.q: When are garden roses usually cut back hard?
99010.e: In spring, when no more hard frost is coming, old and dead shoots are cut off. Afterwards strong new shoots with flowers grow.
99010.m: Roses are cut back in spring.

99011.q: What colour is the rose given as a sign of love?
99011.e: A red rose has long been a sign of love. People give it on Valentine's Day, for example.
99011.m: The red rose is a sign of love.

99012.q: What are many roses known for when you sniff them?
99012.e: Many roses smell sweet and delicate. Their petals are even used to make scented oil.

99013.q: Which fruit belongs to the same plant family as the rose?
99013.e: The rose and the apple both belong to the rose family. Cherries and strawberries are in it too.
99013.m: The apple is related to the rose.

99014.q: How many petals does a simple wild rose usually have?
99014.e: Wild roses such as the dog rose usually have five petals. Garden roses often have many more.
99014.m: A wild rose usually has five petals.

99015.q: What do you cut off roses in summer so that new flowers come?
99015.e: If you cut off faded flowers, the rose puts its strength into new flowers. That way it flowers for longer.
99015.m: Faded rose flowers are cut off.

99016.q: What does a rose in the garden especially need to flower well?
99016.e: Roses love a sunny spot. In the shade they flower much less.

99017.q: What is a rose that grows up walls and arches called?
99017.e: Climbing roses have long shoots. They are tied to trellises, arches or house walls.
99017.m: A climbing rose grows up walls.

99018.q: What do many people call the pelargonium in the window box?
99018.e: The popular balcony flower is really called a pelargonium. But in everyday life most people say geranium.
99018.m: The balcony geranium is really a pelargonium.

99019.q: What are the wild relatives of the geranium that also grow in Swiss meadows called?
99019.e: Geraniums and cranesbills belong to the same plant family. Their fruits look like a long bird's beak.
99019.m: The cranesbill is a wild relative of the geranium.

99020.q: Which continent do most geraniums come from?
99020.e: Most balcony geraniums originally come from southern Africa. It is warm and sunny there.

99021.q: What can geraniums not cope with at all?
99021.e: Geraniums die in frost. That is why they are brought indoors in autumn.
99021.m: Geraniums must be protected from frost.

99022.q: What do geraniums in pots not like at all?
99022.e: Geraniums need regular watering. But if water is left standing in the pot, their roots rot.
99022.m: Geraniums don't like standing water in the pot.

99023.q: What colour are geraniums in Switzerland very often?
99023.e: There are geraniums in red, pink, white and purple. The best known are the red geraniums.
99023.m: Many geraniums have bright red flowers.

99024.q: What happens with some geraniums when you rub their leaves?
99024.e: With scented geraniums, the leaves smell of lemon or rose, for example, when rubbed. That is why they are called that.
99024.m: Scented geraniums smell when you rub their leaves.

99025.q: Which spot do geraniums like best?
99025.e: Geraniums come from a warm, sunny country. They flower most beautifully in the sun.

99026.q: In which season do sunflowers bloom?
99026.e: Sunflowers bloom in summer, when it is warm and sunny. In autumn the seeds then ripen.

99027.q: What does the stem of a sunflower feel like?
99027.e: The stem and leaves of the sunflower are covered in small, stiff hairs. That is why they feel rough.
99027.m: The sunflower's stem is rough and hairy.

99028.q: In what pattern do the seeds sit in a sunflower?
99028.e: The seeds are arranged in many spirals running to the left and to the right. That way a great many seeds fit on the flower head.
99028.m: The sunflower's seeds sit in spirals.

99029.q: Which insects like to collect nectar from sunflowers?
99029.e: The sunflower's many small flowers offer nectar and pollen. That is why bees and bumblebees like to visit them.

99030.q: Which continent does the sunflower come from?
99030.e: The sunflower first grew in North America. Sailors brought it to Europe a long time ago.
99030.m: The sunflower comes from North America.

99031.q: Which animals like eating sunflower seeds at the bird table in winter?
99031.e: Tits and other birds like pecking at sunflower seeds. The seeds give them a lot of energy.

99032.q: How tall can a sunflower in the garden grow?
a: Only as tall as a shoe
99032.e: Many sunflowers grow two to three metres tall. That makes them taller than adults.
99032.m: Sunflowers can grow taller than a person.

99033.q: What does a sunflower need to grow well?
99033.e: As its name says, the sunflower loves the sun. In a bright, warm spot it grows big and strong.

99034.q: What is the big brown centre of the sunflower really?
99034.e: The centre is made of a great many tiny flowers. Each little flower later becomes a seed.
99034.m: The centre of the sunflower is made of many small flowers.

99035.q: Which country does the dahlia come from?
99035.e: Dahlias grow wild in Mexico. There the dahlia is even the national flower.

99036.q: What do dahlias grow from again each year?
99036.e: Dahlias form thick tubers in the ground. New shoots grow from them in spring.

99037.q: How big can the flowers of some dahlias get?
99037.e: There are very large dahlia varieties. Their flowers can get as wide as a plate.
99037.m: Some dahlias have flowers as big as a plate.

99039.e: Dahlias bloom from summer until the first frost. That way they bring colour to the garden in autumn too.
99039.m: Dahlias bloom from summer into autumn.

99040.q: Which flower colour do dahlias not come in?
99040.e: Dahlias come in almost every colour. But there is no truly blue dahlia.
99040.m: There are no truly blue dahlias.

99041.q: What do pompon dahlias look like?
99041.e: Pompon dahlias have lots of rolled-up petals. That is why their flowers are round like little balls.
99041.m: Pompon dahlias are round like balls.

99042.q: Which animals like to nibble young dahlias in spring?
99042.e: Slugs and snails love the tender young shoots of dahlias. That is why gardeners protect the plants well.
99042.m: Slugs and snails like eating young dahlias.

99044.q: What colours are marigold flowers usually?
99044.e: Marigolds glow a strong yellow and orange. Some also have reddish brown spots.
99044.m: Marigolds have yellow and orange flowers.

99045.q: What do the leaves of marigolds smell like?
99045.e: Marigolds have a strong, spicy smell. Some people like it, others don't.

99046.q: Why do gardeners like to plant marigolds between vegetables?
a: To make the vegetables grow faster
99046.e: The roots of marigolds drive away tiny worms in the soil. This keeps the vegetables healthier.
99046.m: Marigolds protect vegetables from pests in the soil.

99047.q: Which country do many marigolds come from?
99047.e: Marigolds originally come from Mexico and Central America. There they are used to decorate big festivals.

99048.q: How long does a marigold in the garden usually live?
99048.e: Most marigolds are annuals. They are sown again every spring.
99048.m: Marigolds are sown again every year.

99049.q: Which creatures especially like eating marigolds?
99049.e: Slugs and snails love marigolds. That is why marigolds can lure them away from other plants.
99049.m: Slugs and snails love eating marigolds.

99050.q: Until when do marigolds bloom in the garden?
99050.e: Marigolds bloom all summer. Only the first frost in autumn ends their flowering.
99050.m: Marigolds bloom until the first frost.

99051.q: When are pansies often planted on the balcony?
99051.e: Pansies cope well with cold. That is why they bloom in early spring, when other flowers are still asleep.

99052.q: What do the markings on many pansy flowers look like?
99052.e: The dark patches in the middle look like a little face. That is why children especially like this flower.
99052.m: Pansies often have a little face.

99053.q: Roughly how tall do pansies grow?
99053.e: Pansies stay small and grow only about 10 to 20 centimetres tall. That is why they fit well in bowls and boxes.

99054.q: What can you do with pansy flowers in the kitchen?
99054.e: Pansy flowers are edible. You can put them on a salad or a cake, for example.

99055.q: How many petals does a pansy have?
99055.e: A pansy has five petals. The bottom petal is the biggest.
